entry: Major deity in [[Hinduism]]. In [[Shaivism]], one of the major traditions within Hinduism, Shiva is the Supreme Lord who creates, protects and transforms the universe. He is known as the Destroyer within the Trimurti, the Hindu trinity that also includes [[Brahma]] and Vishnu. Shiva has benevolent and fierce aspects: he is depicted as an omniscient yogi and as a householder with his wife [[Parvati]] and their sons [[Ganesha]] and Kartikeya, and in fierce forms he slays demons. He is regarded as the patron god of [[Yoga|yoga]], meditation and the arts. Though associated with the Vedic storm god Rudra, he may have non-Vedic roots. He is usually worshiped in the aniconic form of the lingam and is revered across India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Indonesia, especially in [[Java]] and [[Bali]].

Indian ruler, Chhatrapati of the Marathas from 1674 to 1680. He inherited a fiefdom from his father, a general who served the [[Deccan sultanates]], and it later formed the genesis of the [[Maratha Empire|Maratha kingdom]]. Shivaji offered his services to the Mughal emperor [[Aurangzeb]] to invade the declining Sultanate of Bijapur. After a defeat at the Battle of Purandar, he entered vassalage with the [[Mughal Empire]] and was later conferred the title of Raja. He was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad Fort in 1674, despite opposition from local [[Brahmin|Brahmins]]. He employed people of all castes and religions, including Muslims and Europeans, and his forces expanded Maratha influence, built forts and created a Maratha navy. Jyotirao Phule revived his legacy about two centuries after his death. Nationalists such as [[Bal Gangadhar Tilak]] celebrated him, and Hindutva activists later adopted him.

Natural submerged ridge or bank of sand or other loose material that rises from the bed of a body of water to near the surface. Shoals are typically long and narrow, forming where [[River|rivers]], streams or ocean currents deposit [[Sediment|sediment]]. Their shallowness is a danger to [[Navigation|navigation]]. Shoals are also called sandbanks, sandbars, gravelbars or bars in oceanography and geomorphology. They are typically composed of [[Sand|sand]], though they can be any granular matter, such as gravel, shingle or boulders. A shoal may seasonally separate a [[Lagoon|lagoon]] or estuary from the [[Sea|sea]].

Medical condition of insufficient blood flow to the body's tissues, caused by problems with the [[Circulatory system|circulatory system]]. Early symptoms include weakness, elevated heart rate, fast breathing, sweating, anxiety and increased thirst, and complications can progress to confusion, unconsciousness or [[Cardiac arrest|cardiac arrest]]. Shock has four main types: hypovolemic, from [[Bleeding|bleeding]], diarrhea or vomiting; cardiogenic, which may follow a [[Myocardial infarction|heart attack]]; obstructive, from cardiac tamponade or a tension pneumothorax; and distributive, from [[Sepsis|sepsis]], anaphylaxis, upper spinal cord injury or certain overdoses. Diagnosis combines symptoms, [[Physical examination|physical examination]] and laboratory tests. Shock is a medical emergency; emergency help should be called at once, and while waiting the person should be kept warm, with legs raised if possible.

Footwear, normally worn in pairs, that protects and comforts the [[Foot|foot]]. Each shoe is designed to fit either the left foot or the right. Form was originally tied to function, but shoes also became fashion items. Designs range from basic sandals to high fashion shoes by famous designers, and from specialized [[Boot|boots]] for mountaineering or skiing to general-use sneakers. Some shoes, such as steel-toe boots, are required safety equipment at industrial worksites. Shoes were traditionally made of [[Leather|leather]], wood or [[Canvas|canvas]], but are increasingly made of rubber, [[Plastic|plastics]] and other [[Petrochemical|petrochemical]]-derived materials. The shoe industry is worth $200 billion a year, and 90% of shoes end up in [[Landfill|landfills]] because their materials are hard to separate and recycle. The earliest known shoes are sagebrush bark sandals from Fort Rock Cave in [[Oregon]].

Large, stork-like wading bird of tropical East Africa, named for its enormous, shoe-shaped bill. It is also called the whale-headed stork or shoe-billed stork. Although long classified as a [[Stork|stork]], genetic evidence places it with [[Pelican|pelicans]] and [[Heron|herons]] in the order Pelecaniformes. Adults are mainly gray and juveniles browner, and males typically weigh about 5.6 kg (12 lb). Shoebills live in large swamps from [[South Sudan]] to [[Zambia]] and forage alone, ambushing fish, [[Catfish|catfish]] and frogs with a lunge. Breeding pairs build large nests in dense vegetation, and usually only one chick fledges. The species is classified as Vulnerable by the IUCN, with an estimated 3,300–5,300 mature individuals, and its decline is driven by habitat loss and direct threats such as hunting.

Subgenre of [[Alternative rock|alternative rock]] characterized by ethereal soundscapes, obscured vocals and distorted guitar effects. It originated in the late 1980s and early 1990s, mainly among British and Irish bands. The name was coined in 1991 by music executive Andy Ross, who used it to describe the motionless stage presence of bands looking down at their effects pedals. The genre peaked in 1991 with My Bloody Valentine's album *Loveless*, but was overshadowed by American grunge and Britpop. Revivals since the 2000s include nu gaze and, in the 2020s, zoomergaze, a movement led by [[Generation Z|Generation Z]] artists and boosted by [[TikTok|TikTok]].

Title of the military rulers of [[Japan|Japan]] for most of the period 1185–1868. Nominally appointed by the emperor, shoguns usually held real power, except during parts of the Kamakura and [[Sengoku period|Sengoku periods]] when they were figureheads. The title originated among military commanders of the [[Heian period|Heian period]] and was revived in 1185 for Minamoto no Yoritomo, the first shogun in the usual sense. The shogun's officials, called the bakufu, administered the country while the imperial court kept nominal authority. The shogunate lasted nearly 700 years, ending when Tokugawa Yoshinobu surrendered the office to Emperor Meiji in 1867 during the [[Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]].

Japanese [[Baseball|baseball]] player for the [[Los Angeles Dodgers]] of [[Major League Baseball]] (MLB), known as a two-way player who both pitches and hits. He was the first pick of the Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters in the 2012 Nippon Professional Baseball draft. He won American League Most Valuable Player awards in 2021 and 2023. After the 2023 season he signed a 10-year, $700 million contract with the Dodgers, the largest in professional sports history at the time. He was named National League MVP in 2024 and 2025, and the Dodgers won the [[World Series|World Series]] in both years.

Indian Hindi-language action-adventure film of 1975, directed by Ramesh Sippy. It follows two small-time crooks, Veeru (Dharmendra) and Jai ([[Amitabh Bachchan|Amitabh Bachchan]]), who are hired by a retired police officer to capture the bandit Gabbar Singh (Amjad Khan). Filmed in the rocky terrain of Ramanagara in [[Karnataka|Karnataka]], it was released on August 15, 1975, after the Central Board of Film Certification ordered several violent scenes removed. Its initial reviews were negative, but favorable word of mouth made it a box office success, and it ran for more than five years at Mumbai's Minerva Theater. Ranked first in the British Film Institute's 2002 poll of Top 10 Indian films, it is often regarded as one of the greatest Indian films. It is also a defining example of the *masala* film, which mixes several genres, and its dialogue became part of everyday Indian speech.

American television producer, screenwriter and founder of the production company Shondaland. She was the first African American woman to create and serve as showrunner for three television dramas that each reached 100 episodes: [[Grey's Anatomy|Grey's Anatomy]], its spin-off *Private Practice* and the political thriller *Scandal*. Her later credits include *How to Get Away with Murder* and the [[Netflix|Netflix]] series *Bridgerton*. Born in [[Chicago|Chicago]], she earned a bachelor's degree from [[Dartmouth College|Dartmouth College]] in 1991. [[Time (magazine)|Time]] magazine named her to its annual list of the 100 most influential people in 2007, 2013 and 2021.

Competitive and recreational sports focused on accuracy, precision and speed with ranged weapons, mainly [[Firearm|firearms]] such as [[Handgun|handguns]], [[Rifle|rifles]] and [[Shotgun|shotguns]], as well as airguns and bows or [[Crossbow|crossbows]]. Competitions are classified by equipment, distance, target, time limit and degree of athleticism, and team scores are usually the sum of individual scores. Because projectiles can be lethal and noisy, events take place at permanent ranges or temporary fields away from settlements. Target shooting was a favorite sport in colonial America, and in 1871 veteran Union officers formed the National Rifle Association of America to promote rifle shooting on a scientific basis.

Group of shops built together, sometimes under one roof. The first known collections of retailers under one roof were ancient public markets and Middle Eastern bazaars. In [[Paris|Paris]], about 150 covered passages were built between the late 18th century and 1850, and shopping arcades spread across [[Europe|Europe]] in the 19th century. In the [[United States|United States]], the spread of the [[Car|automobile]] in the 1920s led to the first centers with parking. Starting in 1946, larger open-air centers anchored by department stores were built, followed by enclosed malls such as Victor Gruen's Southdale Center near [[Minneapolis|Minneapolis]], which opened in 1956. Many American malls are now in decline or have closed, while successful ones added entertainment, big-box anchor tenants or specialized formats. In Europe, shopping centers continue to grow and thrive.

Activity of examining the goods or services offered by [[Retail|retailers]], with or without intent to buy. The English word derives from [[Old English|Old English]] *sċoppa*, meaning shed, booth, stall or shop. Shopping may be purposeful, or recreational for those who treat it as leisure. Some people shop for hire, such as personal shoppers who advise clients or secret shoppers who evaluate a store for its management or a rival. In antiquity, [[Marketplace|marketplaces]] and fairs were established to exchange goods, and [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greek]] agoras and [[Ancient Rome|Roman]] forums housed merchants' stalls and shops. Online shopping has disrupted the industry, as consumers compare prices and order goods for delivery through sites such as [[Amazon (company)|Amazon]] or China's Alibaba, saving the time and cost of travel.

Track and field event in which an athlete puts, or throws, a heavy spherical ball, the shot, as far as possible. The shot is usually made of [[Iron|iron]] or [[Brass|brass]]; senior men use one weighing 7.260 kg and senior women one weighing 4.000 kg. Men have competed in the [[Summer Olympic Games|Olympic Games]] since 1896 and women since 1948. The event is also part of the [[Decathlon|decathlon]], heptathlon and pentathlon. Athletes throw from a circle 2.135 meters in diameter, using either a glide or a rotational technique and aiming for a release angle under 45°. The men's world record of 23.56 meters was set by Ryan Crouser of the [[United States|United States]] in 2023, and the women's record of 22.63 meters by Natalya Lisovskaya of the [[Soviet Union|Soviet Union]] in 1987.

Smoothbore [[Firearm|firearm]] that fires a shotshell of numerous small pellets, or a single solid slug. Most shotguns have barrels without rifling, and the 12-gauge and 20-gauge are the most common bores. Almost all are breech-loading, in break-action, pump-action or semiautomatic designs. The pellets scatter after leaving the barrel, so each discharge produces a cluster of impacts and effective range is short, which makes shotguns well suited to [[Hunting|hunting]] fast-flying birds. Shotguns were favored by [[Cavalry|cavalry]] in the early to mid-19th century. In [[Trench warfare|trench warfare]] during the First World War, American forces used the pump-action Winchester Model 1897 to great effect. Today shotguns serve in law enforcement, as military breaching tools and for crowd control, and in target sports such as skeet and trap, which use [[Clay|clay]] pigeons.

Hand tool with a broad blade fixed to a medium-length handle, for digging, lifting and moving bulk materials such as [[Soil|soil]], [[Coal|coal]], [[Gravel|gravel]], snow, [[Sand|sand]] or ore. Blades are usually of sheet steel or hard plastic, and handles of wood such as [[Maple|maple]] or fiberglass. Hand shovels are common in [[Agriculture|agriculture]] and are used in [[Archaeology|archaeology]] to excavate subsurface dirt. Ground stone shovels appeared among [[Neolithic|Neolithic]] tools in the Yellow River region of China around 7000–5000 BCE. The round-point shovel suits softer soils, the square-point shovel scoops and transfers material, and the spade has a flat blade for cutting sod. Modern excavators and front-end loaders descend from steam shovels but are not classified as shovels.

Fixture or place in which a person bathes under a spray of typically warm or hot water, with a drain in the floor. Most showers have adjustable temperature, spray pressure and nozzle angle, and a showerhead can be fitted to a [[Bathtub|bathtub]] or small stall with a curtain or door. Showering is more efficient than bathing in a tub, so it is common practice for [[Hygiene|hygiene]]. The ancient Greeks used pressurized water for bathing as early as the 4th century BCE. The first mechanized shower was patented in 1822 by the English inventor William Feetham, though its water was recycled and often unhygienic. By the 1870s French physician François Merry Delabost had introduced communal showers in army barracks and prisons. Late 19th-century gas water heaters made reliable hot water possible for home showers. WaterSense-labeled showerheads reduce flow to 2.0 gallons per minute while keeping pressure.

2001 American animated fantasy comedy film. Loosely based on William Steig's 1990 picture book *Shrek!*, it follows an embittered ogre voiced by [[Mike Myers|Mike Myers]], who makes a pact to rescue Princess Fiona for Lord Farquaad (John Lithgow). Chris Farley was first cast as the title character but died before completing his work, and Myers replaced him. The film parodies [[Fairy tale|fairy tale]] adaptations and helped establish DreamWorks Animation as a competitor to [[Pixar|Pixar]]. It won the first Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, and in 2020 the [[Library of Congress|Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry.

Small, mole-like mammals of the family Soricidae, with 385 known species. Shrews are not rodents, although they resemble long-nosed mice; they are closer relatives of [[Hedgehog|hedgehogs]] and [[Mole (animal)|moles]], and have sharp, spike-like teeth rather than gnawing incisors. Shrews occur almost worldwide, but have no native populations in [[Australia|Australia]], [[New Guinea|New Guinea]] or [[New Zealand|New Zealand]]; [[South America|South America]] has only a relatively recent naturalized population, in the northern [[Andes|Andes]]. The shrew family is the fourth-most species-diverse mammal family. Some species, such as the Etruscan shrew, are among the smallest terrestrial mammals. Shrews are solitary and must eat almost constantly, and the northern short-tailed shrew has [[Venom|venomous]] saliva that immobilizes prey.

[[Passerine|Passerine]] bird family of 34 species in four genera. The family name, and that of the genus *Lanius*, derive from the [[Latin|Latin]] word for butcher, and shrikes are also called butcherbirds because they impale prey on thorns and barbed wire. The English name comes from Old English *scrīc*, alluding to the shrike's shriek-like call. Most species live in open Old World habitats such as [[Savanna|savannas]] and [[Steppe|steppes]] in [[Africa|Africa]] and [[Eurasia|Eurasia]]; only two species are native to North America. Impaled prey serves as food stores and helps attract females. Shrikes hunt insects, lizards, rodents and small birds. Several species have declined, notably the loggerhead shrike in North America, owing to habitat loss and pesticides.

Decapod [[Crustacean|crustacean]] with an elongated body that moves mainly by swimming. Shrimp usually belong to the decapod groups Caridea or Dendrobranchiata. They swim by paddling swimmerets under the abdomen and escape by flicking the tail, which drives them backward in a movement called "lobstering". Unlike [[Crab|crabs]] and [[Lobster|lobsters]], shrimp have thin, fragile legs used mainly for perching. Thousands of species live in freshwater and marine habitats, and they are an important food for fish and [[Whale|whales]]. Most live from one to seven years. Their muscular tails are widely eaten, with about 440 billion farmed and about 25 trillion wild shrimp killed annually. Excessive bycatch and overfishing are significant concerns, and intensive farming has raised concerns over [[Mangrove|mangrove]] deforestation and pollution.

Length of [[Linen|linen]] cloth bearing a faint image of a naked man, venerated by some Christians as the burial shroud of Jesus. The shroud is documented from 1354, when it was exhibited at Lirey, France, and the bishop of Troyes denounced it as a forgery in 1389. It has been kept in [[Turin|Turin]] since 1578, and the image is clearer in negative, a property discovered by Secondo Pia in 1898. In 1988, radiocarbon dating placed the cloth between 1260 and 1390, a result disputed by some defenders. The [[Catholic Church|Catholic Church]] neither endorses nor rejects its authenticity.

Small- to medium-sized perennial woody plant with several stems rising from or near the ground. Shrubs are distinguished from [[Tree|trees]] by their multiple stems and by a height of less than 6–10 m (20–33 ft). Small shrubs under 2 m (6.6 ft) tall are called subshrubs. Some species survive only about five years in good conditions, while larger woody species can live beyond 70 years. Shrubs may be deciduous or evergreen, providing wildlife habitat and food while helping to stabilize soil on slopes. Many garden cultivars are bred for flowers, such as [[Rhododendron|rhododendrons]] and [[Rose|roses]]. Apart from berry-bearing species, few shrubs are eaten directly, but [[Tea|tea]] and coffee are normally harvested from shrub-sized plants, and perfumed species such as lavender are used. A landscape dominated by shrubs is called [[Shrubland|shrubland]].

Plant community dominated by [[Shrub|shrubs]], often also including grasses, herbs and geophytes. Shrubland may be natural or the result of human activity, and it may be a stable mature vegetation type or a transitional community after a disturbance such as fire. It occurs mainly in semi-arid to [[Mediterranean climate|Mediterranean-type climates]] between 30° and 40° latitude, including the Mediterranean Basin, coastal [[California|California]], central [[Chile|Chile]] and [[Western Australia|southwestern Australia]]. Common types include [[Chaparral|chaparral]], sagebrush steppe and South Africa's fynbos. Shrubland species show adaptations to fire, such as heavy seed production, lignotubers and fire-induced germination, and fire danger may make such land unsuitable for habitation. The term was coined in 1903.
